scene: Title card, then the two event calendars: 25 days in 2024, 12 in 2025.
caption: Every December, a website called Advent of Code publishes programming puzzles, one a day: 25 days of them in 2024, and 12 since 2025. I solved them by hand in 2024 and 2025, and kept wondering: could AI models solve them on their own, with no human help? And could I prove it, rather than just claim it?
say: Every December, a website called Advent of Code publishes programming puzzles, one a day: twenty-five days of them in twenty twenty-four, and twelve since twenty twenty-five. I solved them by hand in twenty twenty-four and twenty twenty-five, and kept wondering: could A I models solve them on their own, with no human help? And could I prove it, rather than just claim it?

scene: Three tries, one row each: a program appears, runs, and its result reaches the judge holding the known answer: wrong, an error, correct.
caption: An AI model, the kind behind chatbots like ChatGPT or Claude, is a prediction machine: it guesses what a good answer looks like, and is often wrong. But once a puzzle has been solved, its correct answer is known, so any new answer can be checked instantly and exactly. So each model gets a set number of tries at each puzzle, and each try is a program it writes to solve it. An automatic judge runs every program and checks its answer against the correct one.

scene: One try vs several tries with the judge vs a second model; then the source-of-truth and goal lines.
caption: One question I test: if an AI gets several tries at a puzzle, how much more often does it get it right than with one? And does a second, different model add anything? Previously solved puzzles are the source of truth. The long-term goal is to test AI problem-solving strategies, starting where every answer can be checked: narrow kinds of problems now, broader ones later.

scene: Three columns fill in turn: local models guess, AI assistants helped build it, scripts judge.
caption: The models being tested run locally, so thousands of tries cost nothing extra, and a model can't change in the middle of a test. I built the platform with AI as an engineering partner. And the judging is done by scripts, never by an AI, because it has to be exact.

scene: A puzzle's second part with its first-part story missing; it slides back in. Bar: 6/20 → 19/19.
caption: The biggest surprise was about my own setup. Each puzzle has two parts, and I had been giving the model Part 2 without the Part 1 story it builds on. With that restored, and nothing else changed, one puzzle went from 6 out of 20 to 19 out of 19. What looked like the limit of the AI was mostly missing information.

scene: Dec 1 2026 on the timeline; a Mac at night, 02:00, a run starts.
caption: One catch: past puzzles are public, so a model may have seen their solutions. This year's puzzles, starting December 1st, are newer than every model I use. With the plan written down in advance, my Mac will attempt each one overnight.
